Never fetched by the student's browser until a teacher/marker PDF is generated (formative: automatically when the student clicks Generate; assessed: only via the ?teacher=1-gated action, after Final Submit). Never render any of this on the student-facing page. See CLAUDE.md §5's assessment-security amendment.

markingScheme.criterion: Quotes at least two genuine readings from their own Investigation Record for the same device (wind speed or tidal/current flow speed, and the matching kW), showing the power rose by much more than the speed did.
markingScheme.accept: Any two of the student's own logged readings from the same station with speed and kW (for example 4 m/s with about 218 kW and 8 m/s with about 1,748 kW). Exact figures need not match a model pair, but they must be consistent with the logged record. Noting that power stopped rising because the turbine reached its rated limit is acceptable extra evidence.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'the power went up a lot' or 'it got bigger' with no speeds or kW figures quoted from their own record.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains that power depends on the cube of the speed (more air or water passes each second AND each bit carries more kinetic energy), so doubling the speed gives roughly eight times the power.
markingScheme.accept: Any equivalent scientific wording: 'power is proportional to speed cubed', 'cubed', 'doubling gives about 8×', or 'both the amount of wind per second and the energy of each bit increase, so it rises much faster than the speed'. The exact word 'cube' is not required if the two-factor reasoning or the ×8 result is clearly stated.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating only that 'faster wind has more power' or that power 'doubles' with speed — this restates the observation or gives the wrong relationship without explaining it.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly states whether the hypothesis (written before the investigation) was supported, and links this judgement explicitly to their own evidence.
markingScheme.accept: Any judgement (supported / not supported / partly supported) that is consistent with what their own data shows and that refers back to it. A student who chose a different hypothesis may still earn this mark by honestly judging it against their evidence.
markingScheme.insufficient: Repeating the hypothesis wording without saying whether the evidence agreed with it.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains why wind-only supply would be unreliable: wind speed varies (calms give little or no power, power swings with the cube of speed, and turbines shut down above about 25 m/s), so supply cannot be guaranteed when demand is high.
markingScheme.accept: Any clear statement that wind output depends on the weather and can fall very low in calm periods or stop in storms, linked to the city needing power at specific times (for example the evening peak). Mentioning the cut-in or cut-out speeds or a calm day from the game is a good supporting detail.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying only 'wind is not reliable' or 'wind is bad' with no reason given.

markingScheme.criterion: Names ONE other ocean energy source (tidal stream, ocean current, ocean thermal/OTEC, wave, or floating solar) and explains why it helps by linking a specific property to reliability or complementarity.
markingScheme.accept: Tidal: predictable years ahead because tides follow the Moon and Sun. Ocean current or OTEC: steady day and night, regardless of wind or sun. Wave: often keeps arriving after the wind has dropped (swell lags the wind). Floating solar: strong in the daytime when demand is high. Battery storage alone does not earn this mark because it is not a generation source, though it may be mentioned as additional support.
markingScheme.insufficient: Naming a source with no reason, or a reason that does not connect to reliability (for example 'it is cleaner' or 'it is newer').

markingScheme.criterion: Explains BOTH sides of the pricing trade-off: a price that is too high means households cannot pay (bills unpaid or demand falls), while a price that is too low does not raise enough money to maintain existing units and build new ones.
markingScheme.accept: Equivalent wording for each side, for example 'if bills are too high people cannot afford them', 'if the price is too low there will not be enough income for repairs and new turbines'. Both sides must be present for the mark.
markingScheme.insufficient: Describing only one side (for example only that high prices are bad for households), or stating 'the price should be fair' with no reasons.

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Each question rewards three points, as stated in its marking_scheme in marking_context: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case award it only if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain marking_scheme's 3 points (own-record readings, speed-cubed mechanism, hypothesis judgement), and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply marking_scheme's 3 points (wind-only unreliability, complementary source with a reason, two-sided price trade-off) — the rubric levels restate the same three points as bands at every mark value, never a different route to the same score; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. The Knowledge Check is already auto-marked in auto_marked_score — copy it into knowledge_accuracy (7 marks = full). Use the student's actual logged readings (source / setting / power / hours / kwh / % columns in simulation_results.trials, plus the Harbour Isle Grid run row if present) to verify any figure they claim to quote — do not take their prose summary on trust if it does not match their own logged data. The physics in this activity is simplified: wind power = 0.5 x 1.225 x rotor area x speed^3 x 0.42, capped at 6,000 kW and zero below 3 m/s or above 25 m/s; wave device output = 0.49 x height^2 x period kW per metre x 27 m of effective capture width, capped at 1,500 kW; tidal and ocean-current turbines use the same equation with the density of seawater (1,025 kg/m3). Accept scientifically valid alternative wording and do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 15 (7 auto + 3 + 3 + 2); report the percentage, one strength, one correction, and one next step, in under 80 words.
